title: Natural Key
description: Evaluate business identifiers against fact grain, scope, uniqueness and lifecycle, then audit and enforce a required course-code identity.
notes:
## Identity drawn from the business model

A natural key is an identifying attribute or combination already meaningful in the domain being modeled. A campus course code can identify a course under an institutional policy. A campus code together with a local student number can identify a student if local numbers are only unique within campuses. The identifier has a role beyond being an arbitrary internal row label.

Meaningfulness alone does not establish a key. A student's name is meaningful, yet different students can share it. A course title can describe several offerings. A proposed natural key must satisfy the same identifying and minimality requirements as any candidate key. Start with the actual facts and explicit uniqueness policy rather than assuming that a familiar label is inherently suitable for identification.

## Identify the correct kind of object

A course catalogue entry, a scheduled course offering, and an individual enrollment are different facts. A course code that identifies the catalogue entry does not necessarily identify a particular year's offering. The offering may need a term and section identifier. An enrollment needs to distinguish the participating student as well. A natural identifier can be correct for one level and insufficient for another.

The same issue applies to published items. An externally issued publication identifier can identify the kind of publication it was issued for, but it does not automatically identify every physical copy in a library. Several copies can share that publication identifier while requiring different loan histories. Always state the represented object before presenting an external identifier as a natural-key example.

## Uniqueness requires a defined scope

An institutional course code may be unique across one campus system but reused by another institution. A local registration number may be unique within one campus and reused elsewhere. If the database spans both institutions or campuses, the natural identity may need an additional scope component. A value is not globally unique merely because one department currently treats it as unique.

Historical scope matters too. A code can be retired and later reused for a different catalogue entry. If both historical entries must coexist, the identifier needs an appropriate edition, period, or separate identity policy. Do not silently merge distinct historical facts because their current labels match. A useful natural-key specification explains where and when the issuing authority guarantees identity.

## Current uniqueness is evidence about current data

A sample with no duplicate course codes establishes no observed conflict in that sample. It does not prove the identifier is guaranteed unique across all allowed future records. The policy can be wrong, undocumented, or inconsistently applied. Data-entry errors and imported records can also violate an otherwise valid policy, which is why trusted enforcement remains useful.

Audit repeated values before adding a constraint to existing data. Keep record identifiers in diagnostic output or provide a clear grouped count for investigation. A conflict might indicate duplicated records, a reused identifier, or an incorrect assumption about fact grain. The appropriate correction follows that interpretation; deleting an arbitrary record can destroy legitimate history and does not repair a mistaken identity model.

## Business identifiers can change

A natural identifier can be corrected, reissued, or renamed under a business policy. If child facts reference it directly, that change can affect many relationships. The supported referential actions and transaction strategy determine whether the update is rejected or coordinated. It is inaccurate to claim all natural keys constantly change or that no natural key can ever remain stable; evaluate the actual issuing and correction policy.

A public course code can change while the underlying course identity remains the same. An internal surrogate can decouple related records from that label, leaving the code as a required unique alternate identity if policy still demands it. This is a design choice about lifecycle and callers. A surrogate does not eliminate the need to validate or enforce the natural business identifier.

## Representation needs a comparison policy

A course identifier can contain leading zeros, letters, separators, or case distinctions. Treat it as the documented identifier rather than assuming it is a number suitable for arithmetic. Converting code 007 to integer seven may discard a meaningful representation distinction. Similarly, trimming and case folding should follow an explicit canonicalization policy shared by forms, imports, and lookups.

Stored uniqueness follows applicable comparison rules, including collation for strings. Decide whether db101 and DB101 are equivalent identifiers or distinct codes. A constraint can enforce the selected policy, but its behaviour must match the intended definition. Do not equate visually different spellings with guaranteed distinct database values without checking the actual comparison contract and engine behaviour.

## Meaningful lookup can be convenient

Users often know a course code from a catalogue, so a lookup by that identifier can be convenient. An internal course_id can remain useful for stored references and programmatic selection. A result can return both without forcing users to learn arbitrary numbers. Meaningful identifiers and internal identifiers can coexist when each role and guarantee is clear.

```sql
SELECT course_id, course_title
FROM courses
WHERE course_code = 'DB101';
```

The query assumes a defined required unique course-code policy. It returns no row if the requested code is absent. Searching by title instead is a different contract and can return several courses. A friendly user label should not silently replace the actual identifying predicate when precise selection matters.

## Composite natural identities need every component

If a local course code is only unique within a department, the pair department_code and local_course_code can form a natural identity. The pair permits the same local code in different departments and several courses in one department. Declaring each component independently unique would incorrectly prohibit those legitimate facts. One combined constraint expresses the intended scope.

Minimality still needs checking. If the institution later guarantees every local course code is globally unique, department_code becomes redundant for identification under that stronger rule. The combination remains a superkey but is no longer a minimal candidate key. Logical classification follows the guarantees, not just the fact that a multi-column SQL declaration happens to exist.

## Physical trade-offs need measurements

A long text or composite natural key can make referencing columns and supporting indexes wider. That can affect storage, comparison cost, and access patterns. The impact depends on the actual engine, representation, data distribution, workload, and schema. Avoid presenting every natural key as slower or every integer surrogate as a universal performance solution.

Natural identifiers also offer benefits: they can support recognizable diagnostics, imports, and communication with an issuing system. A wide key might be entirely appropriate for a small reference catalogue. A separate internal key might be more suitable for heavily referenced mutable identities. Compare the actual costs and lifecycle needs rather than choosing solely from a slogan about meaningfulness or speed.

## Enforce the business promise independently

If course_code must identify one required catalogue entry, a suitable UNIQUE and NOT NULL declaration can protect that promise even when course_id is primary. Test a new internal identifier with an existing natural code, a prohibited missing code, and distinct codes sharing the same descriptive title. These cases isolate the natural identity from the internal identity and preserve legitimate repetition.

A code lookup should also define how retired or redirected identifiers are handled. That lifecycle decision belongs in the application contract rather than being guessed from a failed match. The exercises use canonical fixture codes to make comparison expectations explicit. They verify current duplicate detection and local uniqueness enforcement, not external identifier issuance, production authorization, or every provider's behaviour. A dependable natural-key decision states the fact grain, uniqueness scope, absence policy, comparison rules, and lifecycle. With those assumptions visible, meaningful business identifiers can be useful keys without becoming unsupported guarantees about every similarly named column.

questions.question_text: What is a natural key?
options: A key value chosen by a random number generator
A candidate key based on domain-meaningful attributes, possibly a combination
A key that is always numeric
A key with no formal database definition
questions.explanation: Natural keys derive from meaningful real-world attributes, like an ISBN or national ID.

questions.question_text: Which is a plausible natural identifier for a publication edition when the issuing policy guarantees the relevant identity?
options: An auto-incrementing integer id with no external meaning
The edition’s applicable ISBN, rather than a physical library-copy identity
A randomly generated UUID
A row's internal storage address
questions.explanation: The represented object matters: several physical copies can share the publication identifier.

questions.question_text: What is a genuine operational risk of using a natural key as a primary key?
options: Natural keys are always slower to compare than any other data type
The real-world value might need to change later (e.g. a corrected ID), which is painful once other tables have foreign keys pointing at it
Natural keys cannot be indexed
SQL does not allow natural keys as PRIMARY KEY
questions.explanation: Unlike a surrogate key with no business meaning, a natural key's value can legitimately need correction or reissue, creating downstream update problems.

questions.question_text: Why might an assumed natural key turn out to not actually be unique in practice?
options: This never happens with natural keys
Real-world data-entry errors, legacy ID reuse, or coincidental duplicate values can violate an assumption that seemed safe on paper
Natural keys are unique by mathematical law
Only surrogate keys can ever have duplicates
questions.explanation: Real-world data is messier than assumptions — natural keys can have unexpected duplicates that only surface once actually checked or enforced.

questions.question_text: What is one advantage of a natural key over a surrogate key?
options: It requires no design effort and doesn't need to be independently meaningful
It's independently meaningful outside the database, without needing an extra lookup to understand it
It is always shorter to store
It never changes over time
questions.explanation: A natural key already carries real-world meaning, unlike an arbitrary surrogate value.

questions.question_text: How can a natural key negatively affect foreign key performance?
options: Natural keys can never be referenced by foreign keys
If the natural key is long, composite, or an inconvenient type, foreign keys referencing it become wider and potentially slower to index than a compact surrogate integer
Foreign keys referencing natural keys are always faster
This is purely a hypothetical concern with no real basis
questions.explanation: Wider referenced values and indexes can affect costs, but exact performance requires workload and engine evidence.

questions.question_text: Is 'a person's full name' generally considered a reliable natural key?
options: Yes, names are always unique
No — multiple people can share the same name, making it an unreliable choice for uniqueness
Only for people whose names start with a vowel
Names are never allowed as database columns
questions.explanation: Name collisions are common in the real world, making plain name a poor natural-key candidate.

questions.question_text: What is the fundamental trade-off between natural keys and surrogate keys?
options: There is no trade-off; one is strictly better in every case
Natural identities carry business meaning and need scope/lifecycle guarantees; surrogates separate internal identity but do not remove business rules
Surrogate keys are always slower to generate
Natural keys can never be used in a WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Neither approach is universally superior; stability, reference requirements and actual guarantees determine the design.

questions.question_text: Why can a course code identify a catalogue entry but not a particular offering?
options: All codes are invalid
Different terms or sections can offer the same catalogue course
Offerings cannot have keys
A title always identifies the offering
questions.explanation: Fact grain determines the identifying requirements.

questions.question_text: What scope component may be needed when local student numbers repeat across campuses?
options: student_name always
The displayed row number
campus_code
The current score
questions.explanation: The campus-number pair can express scoped identity.

questions.question_text: Does a meaningful student name automatically form a natural key?
options: Yes; all names are unique
Only if sorted alphabetically
No; meaningfulness does not establish uniqueness
Only if stored as text
questions.explanation: A key needs an identifying guarantee as well as domain meaning.

questions.question_text: Why preserve leading zeros when the code contract requires them?
options: Zeros always imply NULL
Every code must be integer
Arithmetic defines identity
Numeric conversion can discard identifier representation distinctions
questions.explanation: An identifier is not automatically a quantity.

questions.question_text: What can explain two historical catalogue entries sharing a current code?
options: The issuing policy may permit code reuse across time
One row must be deleted immediately
Every primary key has failed
Names must be globally unique
questions.explanation: Historical scope may be part of the actual identity.

questions.question_text: Does a surrogate primary key remove required natural-code uniqueness?
options: Yes; generated ids validate codes
No; enforce that independent business rule separately
Only if the code is text
Only if the table is large
questions.explanation: Internal identity does not prevent a business-label collision.

questions.question_text: What can a no-duplicate sample establish?
options: Every future natural identifier is valid
The issuing authority never reuses values
No observed conflict in that sample
A new constraint was applied
questions.explanation: Sample evidence is narrower than a schema guarantee.

questions.question_text: Why inspect collation for string identifiers?
options: Collation always encrypts codes
It creates missing values
It chooses the fact grain
Stored uniqueness can treat different spellings as equivalent
questions.explanation: Comparison behaviour must match identity policy.

questions.question_text: Which claim about natural-key performance is justified without a benchmark?
options: Wider representations can affect costs, but actual impact needs evidence
Every natural key is slower
Every natural key prevents indexes
Every surrogate makes every query faster
questions.explanation: Physical trade-offs depend on engine and workload.

questions.question_text: Why can a publication identifier fail to identify one library copy?
options: Libraries cannot use natural identifiers
Several physical copies can share that publication identity
Every copy is an author
Publication codes are always NULL
questions.explanation: Publication and copy are different fact types.

questions.question_text: Which test isolates a natural-code uniqueness rule?
options: A repeated primary id with a new code only
A repeated descriptive title with distinct codes
A new internal id with an existing required code
A different result alias
questions.explanation: It challenges the alternate business identity independently.

questions.question_text: What must be reviewed before correcting a referenced natural identifier?
options: Only screen order
Only font size
Only the number of characters typed
Its reference dependencies and supported transition policy
questions.explanation: Changing an identity can affect related facts.

coding_problems.title: Audit a proposed institutional course-code identity
coding_problems.task: Return course_code and occurrences for repeated course codes. This is a current-data audit; titles do not define identity.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, course_code VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
constraints: Fixture codes are canonical uppercase spellings with no case-sensitive ambiguity.
edge_cases: Different titles can still conflict on one proposed code.
Repeated titles with distinct codes are not code conflicts.
hints: Group by the proposed business identifier.
Use HAVING to retain counts above one.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT course_code, COUNT(*) AS occurrences FROM courses GROUP BY course_code HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY course_code;
coding_problems.explanation: The grouping detects conflicting current code claims without assuming a title is an identity or prescribing arbitrary deletion.

coding_problems.title: Enforce a required natural identity alongside the internal key
coding_problems.task: Add UNIQUE(course_code) named natural_course_identity to courses. course_id is already primary and course_code already NOT NULL. Return course_id, course_code, course_title, preserving repeated titles.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add natural_course_identity and return the course facts.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, course_code VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
course_id	course_code	course_title
1	DB101	Databases
2	DB201	Databases
constraints: The policy guarantees required course codes unique within this catalogue.
Initial fixture data satisfies the intended rule.
edge_cases: New internal ids cannot justify repeated natural codes.
hints: Use one independent UNIQUE declaration for the natural code.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE courses ADD CONSTRAINT natural_course_identity UNIQUE (course_code);
SELECT course_id, course_code, course_title FROM courses ORDER BY course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The constraint enforces the business-code promise separately from internal row identity. It does not verify external issuance truth.
